Q: How to Perform Conditional Statistics with `Time` Grouping in Apache IoTDB Table Model？ A:

GROUP BY TIME() is not supported in the Table Model of Apache IoTDB 2.0.x. That syntax belongs to the Tree Model, which is why all three of your attempts fail.

In Table Model:

  • Time units like 2s or 2000ms are not recognized.

  • TIME() is not a valid function.

  • Time window grouping must be done using standard SQL-style time bucketing.

To achieve time-based aggregation, you should use DATE_BIN() and specify the interval in milliseconds as an integer.

Here is the correct query for a 2-second window:

SELECT 
  DATE_BIN(2000, time) AS window_start,
  COUNT_IF(value > 15) AS high_value_count
FROM events
GROUP BY DATE_BIN(2000, time)
ORDER BY window_start;

Description:

  • 2000 represents 2000 milliseconds (2 seconds).

  • DATE_BIN(2000, time) groups records into 2-second time buckets.

  • COUNT_IF(value > 15) counts records satisfying the condition within each window.

If you require GROUP BY TIME(2s) syntax, you must use the Tree Model instead. In the Table Model, time-based grouping must be done via DATE_BIN() with millisecond intervals.

Q: Build error in my .net project visual studio 19/22 A:

Try following

  1. Clean & Rebuild the solution

    1. Right click on solution and click on Clean Solution, then Rebuild Solution

  2. Delete temporary compiled/build files

    1. Close all instances of visual studion

    2. Go to project's folder and delete Bin and Obj folders

  3. Delete visual studio's cache files

    1. Close all instances of visual studio

    2. Go to %localappdata%\Microsoft\VisualStudio\[Version]\ComponentModelCache. Replace [Version]with your Visual Studios version, usually 17.0, 18.0 etc

    3. Delete all contents of the folder

Q: What is the maximum length an Intel 386 instruction without any prefixes? A:

The limit without any prefixes is 11. (No 2-byte-opcode instruction takes an imm16/32: http://ref.x86asm.net/coder32.html . So any debate over whether the 0Fh escape-byte counts as a prefix is moot.)

The 386 limit with no redundant or useless prefixes is 15, e.g.
lock add [fs:eax+ebx+disp32],imm32 in 16-bit mode.
Being in 16-bit mode means you get 66h and 67h with SIB and disp32 and imm32, instead of either/or in 32-bit mode. With lock and seg-override prefixes, that's 4 total prefixes plus the base 11, and we're at 15. rep prefixes on 386 don't apply to any instructions that use immediates, or even explicit addressing modes.

So the 15-byte hard limit doesn't stop you from using any encodings of any instruction even in the most extreme corner case on 386. Perhaps that's the reason 386 chose 15 as the limit.

That changed with HLE (Hardware Lock Ellision), part of TSX transactional memory: it introduced xacquire (and xrelease) prefixes, which are the same encoding as rep prefixes but do apply to instructions like lock add. That creates a case where there's a 16-byte encoding that would potentially be useful in a corner case, but isn't valid because of the 15-byte limit. https://www.sandpile.org/x86/opc_enc.htm has examples. (In 16-bit mode with 32-bit addressing and operand-size, or 64-bit mode with 32-bit addressing and a REX prefix.)

Also with XOP, which introduced imm32 for lwp/bextr which aren't 1-byte opcodes. (Intel's BMI1 form of bextr needs the control field in a register not immediate, which is often inconvenient.)

Intel's upcoming APX uses 4-byte EVEX or 2-byte REX2 prefixes to make "legacy" integer instructions 3-operand and allow 32 GPRs, even for instructions that allow disp32 + imm32. This leads to much fairly plausible cases which would be 16 bytes, and corner cases that can be up to 17 bytes with 32-bit addressing, or with HLE + REX2 prefixes. (Again, see the Sandpile link for examples).

The 15 byte #GP limit remains, so you need to avoid those corner cases. e.g. by moving a value into a register with an extra instruction instead of an immediate source, an lea to do some of the address computation. Or avoiding address-size prefixes.

Since the overlong encodings can be avoided, they are not a real life problem.

Q: Get table name of the columns, used only in select statement of the view A:

You can use sys.dm_exec_describe_first_result_set function for this, with the @include_browse_information parameter set to 1.

select
  ed.name,
  CONCAT_WS(N'.',
    ed.source_server
    ed.source_database
    ed.source_schema
    ed.source_table
    ed.source_column) AS source_column
from sys.dm_exec_describe_first_result_set(
  N'SELECT * FROM dbo.YourView', NULL, 1) ed;

You should generally avoid INFORMATION_SCHEMA as it's really only for compatibility and has some inaccuracies.

Q: SQL INSERT OUTPUT to another table A:

(For clarity, I am going to refer to the InputCustomerTypeID as just InputCustomerType or CustomerType, since it really is not an ID value at this point and is more of a type name or type code that still requires a lookup.)

Take a look at this answer to a similar question.

You are on the right track trying to use the OUTPUT clause to capture the inserted ID together with the InputCustomerType from the MigratedCustomer source table. However, you cannot do this in SQL Server using the INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM ... statement, since the output clause cannot directly access columns from the source tables referenced in the FROM clause.

However, the MERGE statement can accomplish this, since its OUTPUT clause can access both the INSERTED columns and the source columns.

I will assume that:

  1. All MigratedCustomer rows are to be inserted. (There are no update-if-present cases.)
  2. All referenced InputCustomerType values already exist in the CustomersType lookup table.

I believe something like the following will accomplish your task:

    MERGE Customer AS TGT
    USING (SELECT * FROM MigratedCustomer) AS SRC
        ON 1 = 0 -- Never match
    WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
        INSERT (InputTitle, InputForename, InputSurname, InputAddress)
        VALUES (SRC.InputTitle, SRC.InputForename, SRC.InputSurname, SRC.InputAddress) 
        OUTPUT INSERTED.ID, SRC.InputCustomerType
            INTO #RowInserted(CustomerId, CustomerType)
    ;

    INSERT INTO CustomersType(CustomerId, CustomerTypeId)
        SELECT RI.CustomerId, CT.ID 
        FROM #RowInserted RI
        JOIN CustType CT
            ON CT.Type = RI.CustomerType;
END

If you have a need to add missing CustType rows as needed from the migration, you can use the following to insert any previously undefined customer types.

INSERT INTO CustType (Type)
SELECT DISTINCT M.InputCustomerType
FROM MigratedCustomer M
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT *
    FROM CustType CT
    WHERE CT.Type = M.InputCustomerType
)
-- AND M.InputCustomerType IS NOT NULL  -- Uncomment this if there might be nulls

The above should be executed sometime before the CustomersType inserts.
